explain.say: A peacock's train is not really his tail but well over a hundred long feathers growing from his back, decorated with shimmering eyespots. Charles Darwin found it puzzling, because it seems to make survival harder.

explain.say: Darwin's answer was sexual selection. Peahens choose which males to mate with, and over generations the males they prefer pass on their genes, so the features they like become bigger and showier.

explain.say: In a famous study, peacocks with more eyespots in their trains mated more often. Later studies found mixed results, so peahens probably also judge the display, the calls and the colours.

A big train may be an honest signal: growing and carrying it costs a lot, so only a healthy, well-fed male can afford a splendid one. In one study, chicks fathered by peacocks with bigger eyespots grew faster and survived better.

faq.a: Sexual selection is evolution driven by competition for mates. When one sex, often females, chooses mates with certain features, those features become more common and more exaggerated over many generations.
asks: What did Darwin say about peacocks?
How does mate choice drive evolution?

faq.q: Why is a big tail a sign of health?
faq.a: A big, bright train takes lots of energy and good food to grow and is hard to carry. A weak or sick male cannot fake one, so it is an honest advertisement of his quality.
asks: Why do peahens like big trains?

faq.a: Peahens sit on their eggs on the ground for about four weeks, so dull brown feathers help them stay hidden from predators. They do the choosing, so they do not need to show off.
asks: Why are female birds often dull?

faq.q: Does the train make it hard to fly?
faq.a: Less than you might think. Peacocks can still take off and fly up into trees to roost, and one study found the train made no big difference to take-off performance.

faq.q: What other animals show off for mates?
faq.a: Birds of paradise dance and display bright plumes, male deer grow antlers to fight rivals, and male fiddler crabs wave one giant claw. All are shaped by sexual selection.

facts: The peacock's train is made of long feathers growing from the back, not from the tail itself.
Peacocks with more eyespots mated more often in a study by Marion Petrie and colleagues (1991).
